claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy is in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution state.
Thermal aging causes the metastable solid solution to undergo nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds.
Mg-rich intermetallic compounds preferentially develop along grain boundaries.
Nucleation, growth, and coalescence of intermetallic compounds redistribute alloying elements.
Intermetallic precipitation locally depletes the surrounding matrix of species that contribute to stable protective oxide formation.
Finely dispersed intermetallic compounds produce local chemistry that enables formation of adherent protective oxide scales.
A finely dispersed and non-percolating intermetallic phase can sustain the resistance of the initial metastable state.
Coarse or interconnected intermetallic compounds undermine the uniformity of the oxide film.
Formation of a coarse or interconnected intermetallic network accelerates corrosion.
Formation of a coarse or interconnected intermetallic network degrades high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Samples retaining finely dispersed intermetallics will have oxide protection similar to or slightly better than the initial state.
Samples developing coarse, interconnected intermetallic networks will show a marked loss of corrosion and oxidation resistance.
The initial metastable solid solution has balanced corrosion and oxidation properties.
Temperatures above approximately 600°C activate the relevant precipitation kinetics.
Sufficiently high temperatures or prolonged exposures cause intermetallic coarsening to progress to a percolated network.
A critical intermetallic size or connectivity threshold separates retention from degradation of protective behavior.
There are no directly reported Mg-containing alloy studies detailing the influence of intermetallic morphology on oxide-formation kinetics.
